# Bayesian Time Series and Dependence {#sec-time-series}



::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives

After this chapter you should be able to:

1. write the likelihood of a time-dependent model by sequential conditioning, and distinguish conditional from exact likelihoods for autoregressions;
2. fit autoregressive models with conjugate priors, impose or check stationarity, and produce forecasts that include parameter uncertainty;
3. formulate latent state (state-space) models, derive the Kalman filter and the prediction-error decomposition of the likelihood, and sample latent states by forward filtering and backward sampling;
4. combine marginal-likelihood MCMC for hyperparameters with exact block sampling of latent states;
5. explain why single-site updating of latent states mixes poorly, and recognise identification problems in dynamic models.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Prerequisites

@thm-gaussian-conditioning (Gaussian conditioning), @sec-regression (conjugate linear regression), @sec-gibbs (blocking), @sec-prediction (predictive distributions), @sec-markov-chains (AR(1) chains).
:::

## Motivation {#sec-ts-motivation}

Observations ordered in time are rarely independent: today's river flow, temperature or case count is informative about tomorrow's. Bayesian time-series models describe this dependence explicitly, either through dependence between observations (autoregressions) or through an unobserved state that evolves over time and generates the observations (state-space models). Two features make them distinctive computationally. The likelihood is built by **sequential conditioning**, and latent-state models contain **as many latent variables as time points**, which must be sampled jointly to avoid very slow mixing. Forecasts, finally, are posterior predictive distributions, and they must include parameter uncertainty to be honest.

## Definitions and notation {#sec-ts-definitions}

For a series $y_{1:n}=(y_1,\dots,y_n)$, any joint density factorises as
$$
p(y_{1:n}\mid\theta)=p(y_1\mid\theta)\prod_{t=2}^np(y_t\mid y_{1:t-1},\theta).
$$ {#eq-sequential-likelihood}
This is the basis of every time-series likelihood.

::: {#def-arp}
## Autoregressive model
The **AR($p$)** model is $y_t=c+\sum_{k=1}^p\phi_ky_{t-k}+\varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t\stackrel{\text{iid}}\sim\mathrm N(0,\sigma^2)$. It is **stationary** if all roots of $1-\phi_1z-\dots-\phi_pz^p$ lie outside the unit circle; for AR(1) this means $\lvert\phi_1\rvert<1$.
:::

::: {#def-state-space}
## Linear Gaussian state-space model: the local level model
An unobserved level $\mu_t$ evolves as a random walk and is observed with noise:
$$
y_t=\mu_t+\varepsilon_t,\quad\varepsilon_t\sim\mathrm N(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2);\qquad\mu_t=\mu_{t-1}+\eta_t,\quad\eta_t\sim\mathrm N(0,\sigma_\eta^2);\qquad\mu_1\sim\mathrm N(m_0,C_0).
$$
The ratio $q=\sigma_\eta^2/\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ is the **signal-to-noise ratio**. More general linear Gaussian state-space models have vector states with linear dynamics and observation equations [@west1997bayesian; @durbin2012time].
:::

## Mathematical development {#sec-ts-development}

### Autoregressions: conditional and exact likelihoods {#sec-ts-ar}

Conditioning on the first $p$ observations, the factors of @eq-sequential-likelihood for $t>p$ are $\mathrm N(y_t\mid c+\sum_k\phi_ky_{t-k},\sigma^2)$. The **conditional likelihood** $\prod_{t=p+1}^np(y_t\mid y_{t-p:t-1})$ is exactly a linear regression likelihood with design rows $(1,y_{t-1},\dots,y_{t-p})$, so the conjugate analysis of @thm-bayes-linear applies unchanged (`ar_design()` builds the design). The **exact likelihood** also includes $p(y_{1:p}\mid\theta)$, the stationary distribution of the first $p$ values. For AR(1) this is $y_1\sim\mathrm N\big(c/(1-\phi),\sigma^2/(1-\phi^2)\big)$, which is only defined for $\lvert\phi\rvert<1$ and destroys conjugacy. For long series the two likelihoods give nearly identical posteriors. For short or nearly non-stationary series they can differ, and the exact likelihood enforces stationarity.

**Stationarity** can be imposed through the prior (restricting $\phi$ to the stationary region, or reparameterising through partial autocorrelations [@monahan1984note]), or *checked* afterwards by computing the posterior probability of the stationary region from posterior draws. The latter is useful when non-stationarity is scientifically plausible and should be allowed to show itself.

### Forecasting {#sec-ts-forecasting}

The $h$-step-ahead predictive distribution is
$$
p(y_{n+h}\mid y_{1:n})=\int p(y_{n+h}\mid y_{1:n},\theta)\,\pi(\theta\mid y_{1:n})\,d\theta,
$$
computed by simulation: for each posterior draw $\theta^{(s)}$, simulate the model forward from the observed end of the series. The resulting fan of paths includes both the accumulating innovation noise and parameter uncertainty. Plug-in forecasts at a point estimate omit the latter, which for persistent processes ($\phi$ near 1) grows with the horizon.

### State-space models and the Kalman filter {#sec-ts-kalman}

For the local level model, the filtering distributions $p(\mu_t\mid y_{1:t})$ are Gaussian and can be computed recursively.

::: {#thm-kalman}
## Kalman filter and prediction-error decomposition
For the local level model with known variances, let $\mu_{t-1}\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N(m_{t-1},C_{t-1})$. Then:

1. (**predict**) $\mu_t\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N(a_t,R_t)$ with $a_t=m_{t-1}$, $R_t=C_{t-1}+\sigma_\eta^2$; and $y_t\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N(a_t,Q_t)$ with $Q_t=R_t+\sigma_\varepsilon^2$;
2. (**update**) $\mu_t\mid y_{1:t}\sim\mathrm N(m_t,C_t)$ with $K_t=R_t/Q_t$, $m_t=a_t+K_t(y_t-a_t)$ and $C_t=(1-K_t)R_t$;
3. (**likelihood**) $\log p(y_{1:n})=\sum_{t=1}^n\log\mathrm N(y_t\mid a_t,Q_t)$, with $a_1=m_0$ and $R_1=C_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1) $\mu_t=\mu_{t-1}+\eta_t$ with $\eta_t$ independent of $y_{1:t-1}$ and of $\mu_{t-1}$, so the predictive distribution of $\mu_t$ is the sum of independent Gaussians; similarly $y_t=\mu_t+\varepsilon_t$. (2) Given $y_{1:t-1}$, $(\mu_t,y_t)$ is bivariate normal with means $(a_t,a_t)$, variances $(R_t,Q_t)$ and covariance $R_t$, and @thm-gaussian-conditioning gives $\mu_t\mid y_t,y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N\big(a_t+\frac{R_t}{Q_t}(y_t-a_t),\ R_t-\frac{R_t^2}{Q_t}\big)$. (3) This is @eq-sequential-likelihood with the predictive densities from (1).
:::

Part (3), the **prediction-error decomposition**, evaluates the likelihood of the variance parameters with the states integrated out, in $O(n)$ operations [@kalman1960new; @durbin2012time]. `tests/testthat/test-time-series.R` checks it against the dense $n$-dimensional Gaussian density of $y$.

### Sampling the latent states jointly {#sec-ts-ffbs}

The states can be sampled jointly from $p(\mu_{1:n}\mid y,\sigma_\varepsilon^2,\sigma_\eta^2)$ by running the filter forwards and sampling backwards.

::: {#thm-ffbs}
## Forward filtering, backward sampling
For the local level model,
$$
p(\mu_{1:n}\mid y_{1:n})=p(\mu_n\mid y_{1:n})\prod_{t=1}^{n-1}p(\mu_t\mid\mu_{t+1},y_{1:t}),
$$
with $\mu_n\mid y_{1:n}\sim\mathrm N(m_n,C_n)$ and $\mu_t\mid\mu_{t+1},y_{1:t}\sim\mathrm N\big(m_t+B_t(\mu_{t+1}-m_t),\ (1-B_t)C_t\big)$, $B_t=C_t/(C_t+\sigma_\eta^2)$. Drawing $\mu_n$ first and then $\mu_{n-1},\dots,\mu_1$ in turn gives an exact joint draw [@carter1994gibbs; @fruhwirth1994data].
:::

::: {.proof}
By the chain rule, $p(\mu_{1:n}\mid y_{1:n})=p(\mu_n\mid y_{1:n})\prod_{t<n}p(\mu_t\mid\mu_{t+1:n},y_{1:n})$. Given $\mu_{t+1}$, the state $\mu_t$ is conditionally independent of $\mu_{t+2:n}$ and $y_{t+1:n}$, since these depend on $\mu_t$ only through $\mu_{t+1}$ (the model is a Markov chain with conditionally independent observations). So $p(\mu_t\mid\mu_{t+1:n},y_{1:n})=p(\mu_t\mid\mu_{t+1},y_{1:t})\propto\mathrm N(\mu_t\mid m_t,C_t)\,\mathrm N(\mu_{t+1}\mid\mu_t,\sigma_\eta^2)$, the product of the filtering density and the transition density. Completing the square gives the stated normal distribution, as in @prp-normal-known with "prior" $\mathrm N(m_t,C_t)$ and "observation" $\mu_{t+1}$ of variance $\sigma_\eta^2$.
:::

FFBS costs $O(n)$ per draw and produces states that are *independent* across iterations given the variances. A **single-site Gibbs sampler**, which updates each $\mu_t$ given its neighbours $\mu_{t-1},\mu_{t+1}$ and $y_t$, is also valid. It mixes very slowly when $q$ is small, because neighbouring states are then strongly dependent: each $\mu_t$ is pinned by its neighbours, and information propagates along the series one step at a time. This is the bivariate-normal phenomenon of @prp-gibbs-bvn in $n$ dimensions, and the reason blocking matters in time series.

### MCMC for the hyperparameters {#sec-ts-mcmc}

The variances $(\sigma_\varepsilon^2,\sigma_\eta^2)$ have no conjugate posterior with the states integrated out. A good strategy combines:

1. **marginal MCMC** for $(\log\sigma_\varepsilon,\log\sigma_\eta)$, a two-dimensional target evaluated by the Kalman filter likelihood (@thm-kalman) plus priors and log-Jacobians, sampled by random-walk Metropolis;
2. **exact FFBS draws** of the states for each retained draw of the variances.

The pair gives exact posterior draws of everything, up to the Markov chain's Monte Carlo error for the variances only, because $p(\mu,\sigma\mid y)=p(\sigma\mid y)\,p(\mu\mid\sigma,y)$. This "collapse, then reconstruct" strategy is far more efficient than Gibbs sampling states and variances alternately, which suffers from the strong posterior dependence between the states and $\sigma_\eta$ [@carter1994gibbs].

For non-Gaussian or non-linear state-space models (stochastic volatility, count time series), the filter is not available in closed form. Options include data-augmentation schemes that make the model conditionally Gaussian [@kim1998stochastic], particle filters [@gordon1993novel] and particle MCMC [@andrieu2010particle] (@sec-specialized).

### Identification challenges {#sec-ts-identification}

- **Signal and noise.** In the local level model, slowly varying levels with noisy observations ($q$ small) and rapidly varying levels with little noise can describe a short series about equally well. The posterior of $(\sigma_\varepsilon,\sigma_\eta)$ can then be strongly correlated or banana-shaped, and is sensitive to the priors.
- **Non-stationarity versus long memory.** A near-unit-root AR(1) and a local level model can be hard to distinguish, and forecasts at long horizons depend heavily on which is assumed.
- **Label switching and multimodality** in hidden Markov and regime-switching models, where states can be relabelled without changing the likelihood [@jasra2005markov].
- **Initial conditions.** Diffuse priors on the initial state ($C_0$ large) are standard, but they make the marginal likelihood depend on the arbitrary $C_0$, which matters for model comparison (@sec-model-comparison) though not for the posterior of the variances.

## Worked example 1: the Nile river {#sec-ts-worked-nile}

The `Nile` series records the annual flow of the Nile at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, in units of $10^8$ m³ [@durbin2012time; @cobb1978problem; @balke1993detecting]. A drop in level around 1899 is attributed to the construction of the first Aswan dam and to climatic changes.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
y <- as.vector(Nile); yrs <- 1871:1970
log_post_var <- function(ls) {                     # ls = (log sigma_eps, log sigma_eta)
  se <- exp(ls[1]); sn <- exp(ls[2])
  kalman_local_level(y, se^2, sn^2, m0 = 1000, C0 = 1e7)$loglik +
    sum(dnorm(c(se, sn), 0, 500, log = TRUE)) + sum(ls)   # half-normal(0, 500) priors + log-Jacobians
}
set.seed(2201)
chains <- lapply(1:4, function(k) rw_metropolis(log_post_var, c(log(100), log(40)) + rnorm(2, 0, 0.5), 6000,
                                                proposal_cov = 0.15^2 * matrix(c(1, -0.5, -0.5, 1), 2)))
sig <- lapply(chains, function(ch) exp(ch$draws[-(1:1000), ]))
se <- sapply(sig, function(d) d[, 1]); sn <- sapply(sig, function(d) d[, 2])
rbind(summarise_draws_basic(se, "sigma_eps"), summarise_draws_basic(sn, "sigma_eta"),
      summarise_draws_basic(sn^2 / se^2, "signal_to_noise_q"))
#>            variable     mean      sd        q5      q95  rhat ess_bulk
#> 1         sigma_eps 122.3124 12.6676 102.10589 143.5111 1.001   1286.7
#> 2         sigma_eta  44.6810 16.4161  21.95559  75.4567 1.007    373.6
#> 3 signal_to_noise_q   0.1715  0.1725   0.02706   0.4952 1.006    399.6
#>   ess_tail mcse_mean
#> 1   2421.8  0.352366
#> 2    580.7  0.824802
#> 3    661.7  0.007376
```
:::


For comparison, the maximum likelihood estimates reported by @durbin2012time for this model are $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2=15099$ and $\hat\sigma_\eta^2=1469.1$, i.e. $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon\approx123$ and $\hat\sigma_\eta\approx38$. The posterior is centred close to these values, and it shows how uncertain the level variance is: its 90% interval spans a factor of about three.

**Smoothed level and forecasts.** For a subset of the posterior draws of the variances, draw the whole level path by FFBS, then simulate ten years ahead:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2202)
all_sig <- do.call(rbind, sig); idx <- sample(nrow(all_sig), 1000)
paths <- t(sapply(idx, function(k) ffbs_local_level(y, all_sig[k, 1]^2, all_sig[k, 2]^2, 1000, 1e7)))
H <- 10
fc <- t(sapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
  lev <- paths[i, 100] + cumsum(rnorm(H, 0, all_sig[idx[i], 2]))
  lev + rnorm(H, 0, all_sig[idx[i], 1])
}))
band <- function(m) apply(m, 2, quantile, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
L <- band(paths); Fb <- band(fc); fy <- 1971:1980
plot(yrs, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = course_ink, xlim = c(1871, 1980), ylim = c(300, 1500), xlab = "year", ylab = "flow")
polygon(c(yrs, rev(yrs)), c(L[1, ], rev(L[3, ])), col = alpha_col(course_cols[["blue"]], 0.25), border = NA)
lines(yrs, L[2, ], col = course_cols[["blue"]], lwd = 2)
polygon(c(fy, rev(fy)), c(Fb[1, ], rev(Fb[3, ])), col = alpha_col(course_cols[["orange"]], 0.25), border = NA)
lines(fy, Fb[2, ], col = course_cols[["orange"]], lwd = 2)
abline(v = 1899, lty = 3, col = course_muted)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Nile flow (points) with the posterior median of the latent level (blue line) and its 90% band, from FFBS draws averaged over the posterior of the variances, followed by a 10-year predictive median and 90% band (orange) for the flow.](22-time-series_files/figure-html/fig-ts-nile-level-1.png){#fig-ts-nile-level fig-align='center' width=92%}
:::
:::


The smoothed level falls steeply around 1899, consistent with the known change, without the model having been told about it. A random-walk level can accommodate a shift through one or two large innovations. The 10-year forecast band widens with the horizon, because future level changes accumulate ($\operatorname{Var}=h\sigma_\eta^2+\sigma_\varepsilon^2$), averaged over the posterior uncertainty in both variances. A model with an explicit change point or a different level process would give different long-range forecasts. Comparing such models is the subject of @sec-model-comparison.

## Worked example 2: Lake Huron, an AR(2) model {#sec-ts-worked-huron}

The `LakeHuron` series gives the annual level of Lake Huron (feet) from 1875 to 1972 [@brockwell1991time]. We centre the series at its sample mean, so that the intercept $c$ is near zero and the priors are easy to state, and fit an AR(2) model by the conditional likelihood with a weak conjugate prior. (Centring matters: in the parameterisation $y_t=c+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\phi_2y_{t-2}+\varepsilon_t$, the intercept is $c=\mu(1-\phi_1-\phi_2)$, not the mean $\mu$, so a prior "centred at the mean" on $c$ would be badly misspecified and would distort the estimates of $\phi$.)


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
yh <- as.vector(LakeHuron); ybar <- mean(yh); d <- ar_design(yh - ybar, 2)
fit <- conjugate_linear_regression(d$X, d$y, m0 = c(0, 0, 0), V0 = diag(c(100, 1, 1)), a0 = 1, b0 = 1)
set.seed(2203)
dr <- fit$draw(20000)
stationary <- apply(dr[, c("phi1", "phi2")], 1, ar_is_stationary)
rbind(post_mean = colMeans(dr), q05 = apply(dr, 2, quantile, 0.05), q95 = apply(dr, 2, quantile, 0.95)) |> round(3)
#>                c  phi1   phi2 sigma2
#> post_mean -0.024 0.998 -0.216  0.486
#> q05       -0.141 0.839 -0.376  0.382
#> q95        0.094 1.158 -0.055  0.613
c(P_stationary = mean(stationary), arima_phi = round(coef(arima(yh, order = c(2, 0, 0), method = "CSS"))[1:2], 3))
#>  P_stationary arima_phi.ar1 arima_phi.ar2 
#>        0.9999        1.0220       -0.2380
```
:::


The posterior places essentially all of its mass in the stationary region, so a stationarity constraint would barely change the results. The posterior means are close to the conditional-sum-of-squares estimates from `arima()`, slightly shrunk by the prior. Forecasts with and without parameter uncertainty:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
H <- 15; n <- length(yh); keep <- which(stationary)[1:4000]
yc <- yh - ybar
sim_ar <- function(b, s2) { z <- c(yc[n - 1], yc[n]); out <- numeric(H)
  for (h in 1:H) { nxt <- b[1] + b[2] * z[2] + b[3] * z[1] + rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(s2)); out[h] <- nxt; z <- c(z[2], nxt) }
  out + ybar }
full <- t(sapply(keep, function(k) sim_ar(dr[k, 1:3], dr[k, "sigma2"])))
plug <- t(replicate(4000, sim_ar(colMeans(dr[, 1:3]), mean(dr[, "sigma2"]))))
fb <- band(full); pb <- band(plug); fyrs <- 1973:(1972 + H)
plot(1875:1972, yh, type = "l", col = course_ink, xlim = c(1940, 1972 + H), ylim = c(574, 584), xlab = "year", ylab = "level (ft)")
polygon(c(fyrs, rev(fyrs)), c(fb[1, ], rev(fb[3, ])), col = alpha_col(course_cols[["orange"]], 0.3), border = NA)
lines(fyrs, fb[2, ], col = course_cols[["orange"]], lwd = 2)
lines(fyrs, pb[1, ], lty = 2, col = course_muted); lines(fyrs, pb[3, ], lty = 2, col = course_muted)
c(width_h15_full = diff(fb[c(1, 3), H]), width_h15_plugin = diff(pb[c(1, 3), H]))
#>   width_h15_full.95% width_h15_plugin.95% 
#>                4.337                4.155
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Lake Huron: 15-year predictive 90% bands from the full posterior (orange) and from a plug-in forecast at the posterior mean (dashed). With 98 observations, parameter uncertainty widens the long-horizon band only modestly.](22-time-series_files/figure-html/fig-ts-huron-forecast-1.png){#fig-ts-huron-forecast fig-align='center' width=92%}
:::
:::


Here the full predictive band at 15 years is only about 4% wider than the plug-in band: with 98 observations, innovation noise dominates the forecast uncertainty. The difference grows for shorter series and for persistence closer to a unit root (@exr-ts-6), which is exactly when plug-in forecasts are most misleading.

## R implementation {#sec-ts-r}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Time-series models (Chapter 22) ------------------------------------------------------

#' Design matrix for an AR(p) model with intercept, conditioning on the first p
#' observations: y_t = c + phi_1 y_{t-1} + ... + phi_p y_{t-p} + e_t, t = p+1..n.
ar_design <- function(y, p) {
  check_finite_vector(y, "y"); p <- check_count(p, "p")
  n <- length(y)
  if (n <= p + 1) course_stop("Series too short for AR(%d).", p)
  X <- cbind(1, sapply(seq_len(p), function(k) y[(p + 1 - k):(n - k)]))
  colnames(X) <- c("c", paste0("phi", seq_len(p)))
  list(X = X, y = y[(p + 1):n])
}

#' Is an AR(p) coefficient vector stationary? (all roots of 1 - phi_1 z - ... - phi_p z^p
#' lie outside the unit circle)
ar_is_stationary <- function(phi) all(Mod(polyroot(c(1, -phi))) > 1)

#' Kalman filter for the local level model
#'   y_t = mu_t + eps_t,   eps_t ~ N(0, s2_eps)
#'   mu_t = mu_{t-1} + eta_t, eta_t ~ N(0, s2_eta),   mu_1 ~ N(m0, C0).
#' Returns filtered means m_t, variances C_t, one-step predictive means f_t and
#' variances Q_t, and the log-likelihood log p(y_1..y_n | s2_eps, s2_eta) by the
#' prediction-error decomposition  sum_t log N(y_t | f_t, Q_t).
kalman_local_level <- function(y, s2_eps, s2_eta, m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7) {
  n <- length(y)
  m <- C <- f <- Q <- numeric(n)
  a <- m0; R <- C0                                  # prior for mu_1
  loglik <- 0
  for (t in seq_len(n)) {
    if (t > 1) { a <- m[t - 1]; R <- C[t - 1] + s2_eta }   # predict state
    f[t] <- a; Q[t] <- R + s2_eps                          # predict observation
    K <- R / Q[t]                                          # Kalman gain
    m[t] <- a + K * (y[t] - f[t]); C[t] <- (1 - K) * R      # update
    loglik <- loglik + stats::dnorm(y[t], f[t], sqrt(Q[t]), log = TRUE)
  }
  list(m = m, C = C, f = f, Q = Q, loglik = loglik)
}

#' Forward-filtering backward-sampling (Carter and Kohn, 1994; Fruhwirth-Schnatter, 1994):
#' one joint draw of mu_1..mu_n from p(mu | y, s2_eps, s2_eta). Backward step:
#'   mu_n ~ N(m_n, C_n);  mu_t | mu_{t+1}, y_{1:t} ~ N(m_t + B_t (mu_{t+1} - m_t), C_t (1 - B_t)),
#'   B_t = C_t / (C_t + s2_eta).
ffbs_local_level <- function(y, s2_eps, s2_eta, m0 = 0, C0 = 1e7, kf = NULL) {
  if (is.null(kf)) kf <- kalman_local_level(y, s2_eps, s2_eta, m0, C0)
  n <- length(y); mu <- numeric(n)
  mu[n] <- stats::rnorm(1, kf$m[n], sqrt(kf$C[n]))
  for (t in (n - 1):1) {
    B <- kf$C[t] / (kf$C[t] + s2_eta)
    mu[t] <- stats::rnorm(1, kf$m[t] + B * (mu[t + 1] - kf$m[t]), sqrt(kf$C[t] * (1 - B)))
  }
  mu
}
```
:::


The Kalman filter runs in $O(n)$ and returns the log-likelihood used inside the Metropolis sampler for the variances. FFBS reuses the filter output, so drawing a full path of 100 states costs about as much as one likelihood evaluation. The tests compare the filter's log-likelihood with the dense multivariate normal density of $y$, and the FFBS draws' means and variances with the exact Gaussian smoothing distribution computed by direct conditioning.

## Computational experiment: single-site Gibbs versus FFBS {#sec-ts-experiment}

With the variances fixed at their maximum likelihood values, compare the single-site Gibbs sampler for the 100 states with FFBS, measuring the ESS of the state in 1899 and of the average level.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
s2e <- 15099; s2n <- 1469.1; n <- length(y)
single_site <- function(n_iter, mu = rep(mean(y), n)) {
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, n_iter, n)
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    for (t in 1:n) {
      # full conditional of mu_t: prior from neighbours (random walk) times likelihood of y_t
      if (t == 1)      { pm <- mu[2];                 pv <- s2n }      # diffuse mu_1 prior ignored (C0 huge)
      else if (t == n) { pm <- mu[n - 1];             pv <- s2n }
      else             { pm <- (mu[t - 1] + mu[t + 1]) / 2; pv <- s2n / 2 }
      v <- 1 / (1 / pv + 1 / s2e); mu[t] <- rnorm(1, v * (pm / pv + y[t] / s2e), sqrt(v))
    }
    out[it, ] <- mu
  }
  out
}
set.seed(2204)
ss <- single_site(3000)[-(1:500), ]
kf <- kalman_local_level(y, s2e, s2n, 1000, 1e7)
fb <- t(replicate(2500, ffbs_local_level(y, s2e, s2n, 1000, 1e7, kf = kf)))
rbind(single_site = c(ess_mu1899 = ess_bulk(ss[, 29]), ess_mean_level = ess_bulk(rowMeans(ss)),
                      mean_mu1899 = mean(ss[, 29])),
      ffbs = c(ess_bulk(fb[, 29]), ess_bulk(rowMeans(fb)), mean(fb[, 29])))
#>             ess_mu1899 ess_mean_level mean_mu1899
#> single_site        231          110.5       953.8
#> ffbs              2382         2401.8       951.1
```
:::


Both samplers target the same distribution and their estimates agree, but the single-site sampler's ESS for the average level is a small fraction of FFBS's from the same number of iterations. Its sweeps are also more expensive in R, because of the loop over time points. Smooth, slowly varying functions of the states, such as the average level, mix worst under single-site updating, because they depend on long-range coordination that local moves achieve only slowly.

## Diagnostics and validation {#sec-ts-validation}

- **Exact checks** for the Kalman filter and FFBS against dense Gaussian computations (the test file).
- **Residual checks**: the standardised one-step prediction errors $(y_t-a_t)/\sqrt{Q_t}$ should be approximately independent standard normal under the model. Plot them, and check their autocorrelation and their distribution for outliers (the Nile series has a few).
- **Posterior predictive checks** for time series should use test quantities sensitive to dependence: autocorrelations, run lengths, and the number of large changes.
- **Out-of-sample forecast evaluation**: score forecasts of held-out years with the log score or CRPS (@sec-pred-scores), using a rolling origin.
- **Sampler diagnostics** for the hyperparameters as usual, with special attention to strong posterior correlation between variance components.

## Interpretation {#sec-ts-interpretation}

The local level model describes the Nile series as a slowly wandering mean observed with substantial noise. The posterior quantifies how much of the variation is signal (level changes) and how much is noise, and that split determines how much the smoothed level follows individual observations and how fast forecast uncertainty grows. The Lake Huron AR(2) model is stationary, so its forecasts revert towards a long-run mean. Including parameter uncertainty widens long-horizon bands, modestly here, and more for shorter or more persistent series. In both cases the forecast distribution is the model's honest statement about the future *if the model is right*, and checking it on held-out data is the only way to learn whether it is.

## Limitations and common errors {#sec-ts-errors}

- **Treating time-series observations as independent**, which understates uncertainty (@sec-pred-worked found this for the discoveries series).
- **Plug-in forecasts** that ignore parameter uncertainty.
- **Single-site Gibbs sampling of latent states** when block sampling is available.
- **Using the conditional likelihood for short series** without considering the initial values.
- **Ignoring identification problems** between variance components, or between non-stationarity and persistent dynamics.
- **Diffuse initial-state priors in model comparison**: marginal likelihoods then depend on arbitrary constants.

## Chapter summary {#sec-ts-summary}

- Time-series likelihoods factorise by sequential conditioning (@eq-sequential-likelihood). AR($p$) models with the conditional likelihood are linear regressions, so the conjugate analysis applies.
- Stationarity can be imposed through the prior or checked from posterior draws. Forecasts are simulated from the posterior predictive distribution and include parameter uncertainty.
- The Kalman filter (@thm-kalman) gives filtering distributions and the marginal likelihood of linear Gaussian state-space models in $O(n)$. FFBS (@thm-ffbs) samples all states jointly.
- Marginal MCMC for hyperparameters plus exact state draws is far more efficient than single-site or alternating Gibbs sampling.
- Identification problems (signal versus noise, persistence versus non-stationarity, label switching) are common in dynamic models and must be examined, not assumed away.

## Solutions {#sec-ts-solutions}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-1
$\log p(y_{1:n})=\log\mathrm N\big(y_1\mid\frac c{1-\phi},\frac{\sigma^2}{1-\phi^2}\big)+\sum_{t=2}^n\log\mathrm N(y_t\mid c+\phi y_{t-1},\sigma^2)$. The difference from the conditional log-likelihood is the single first term, which is $O(1)$ in $n$. It matters for small $n$, and it becomes $-\infty$-like as $\lvert\phi\rvert\to1$ (the stationary variance diverges), which is how it enforces stationarity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-2
If $\theta_{t-1}\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N(m_{t-1},C_{t-1})$, then $\theta_t\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N(a_t,R_t)$ with $a_t=Gm_{t-1}$, $R_t=GC_{t-1}G^\top+W$; $y_t\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim\mathrm N(f_t,Q_t)$ with $f_t=F^\top a_t$, $Q_t=F^\top R_tF+V$; and the joint covariance of $(\theta_t,y_t)$ is $R_tF$. By @thm-gaussian-conditioning, $m_t=a_t+R_tFQ_t^{-1}(y_t-f_t)$ and $C_t=R_t-R_tFQ_t^{-1}F^\top R_t$ [@west1997bayesian, Chapter 4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-3
The exact log-likelihood adds $\log\mathrm N(y_1\mid c/(1-\phi),\sigma^2/(1-\phi^2))$. Sample $(c,\phi,\log\sigma)$ by RWM with a log target returning $-\infty$ for $\lvert\phi\rvert\ge1$. With 98 observations the posteriors of $\phi$ from the two likelihoods are very similar (posterior mean around 0.8), and slightly different near the upper tail, where the exact likelihood's penalty on near-unit roots acts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-4
Use `kf <- kalman_local_level(y, median(se)^2, median(sn)^2, 1000, 1e7)` and `e <- (y - kf$f) / sqrt(kf$Q)`. The largest standardised errors occur around 1899 (the level shift) and in a few extreme years (e.g. 1913, a very low flow). A model with an explicit intervention at 1899, or with heavy-tailed observation noise, would accommodate them better [@durbin2012time].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-5
With $q=0.01$ the level barely moves, and the data struggle to distinguish a slightly larger $\sigma_\eta$ (with correspondingly smaller $\sigma_\varepsilon$) from the truth. The posterior of $(\log\sigma_\varepsilon,\log\sigma_\eta)$ is elongated and negatively correlated, and $\sigma_\eta$'s posterior is wide and prior-sensitive. With $q=1$ both variances are well identified and the correlation is weaker. Signal and noise trade off when the signal is weak.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-6
The intervals ignore uncertainty in $\hat\phi$ and $\hat\sigma$ (and in the mean). With $\hat\phi=0.97$, plausible values range from about 0.9 to 1 (or beyond), which changes long-horizon forecasts dramatically: near-unit-root uncertainty makes the predictive variance grow much faster than the plug-in formula suggests. A Bayesian analysis simulates future paths for each posterior draw of $(c,\phi,\sigma)$, so the predictive intervals include parameter uncertainty and, if the prior allows it, the possibility of non-stationarity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-ts-7
The bootstrap filter propagates $N$ particles through the state equation, weights them by $\mathrm N(y_t\mid\mu_t^{(i)},\sigma_\varepsilon^2)$, accumulates $\log\frac1N\sum_iw_t^{(i)}$, and resamples. Its likelihood estimate is unbiased on the natural scale, and its log has a negative bias and a variance that shrinks roughly like $1/N$. With $N=100$ the standard deviation of the log-likelihood estimate is around 1–2, and with $N=1000$ it is several times smaller. Used inside Metropolis–Hastings (PMMH), the chain targets the exact posterior because the estimate is unbiased [@andrieu2009pseudo], but it sticks when the estimate happens to be high. A standard deviation of the log-likelihood estimate around 1–1.5 is a common working target.
:::
